output.title: Privacy promises are not the same as workflow control
output.body:
If you are considering AI in a small business, privacy promises are only one part of the question. A vendor can tell you where data is stored, how it is protected, or what terms apply. That still does not answer the more practical issue: who can do what inside your workflow once the data is there.

That is the bounded decision to make first. For a repeatable process such as invoice handling or customer replies, decide whether the AI may act on its own, or whether it only recommends an action and waits for human approval. For money movement and other high-risk decisions, human approval stays mandatory. That is policy, not wishful thinking.

This matters because privacy expectations do not control your own approval design. If the workflow is loose, the safest vendor in the world will not fix that. If the workflow is tight, you can use AI without handing over the keys to the shop.

A simple question helps: will I see the input, the reasoning, and the recommended action before anything is committed?

The next step is to map your most repeated workflow, mark the points where money, customer communication, or data deletion could happen, and decide which of those points must remain human-approved. If you are working with invoice handling, keep in mind that Bareni’s account-payable demo is synthetic and its blocked payment step is a manual simulation, not a real transfer. Human approval remains the rule at the top level.
